newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US, rate hopes offset Dow slide.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US, rate hopes offset Dow slide.

text.p: The dollar closed mixed as market players weighed their hopes for higher short-term interest rates against the risk posed by sharp declines in U.S. financial markets on Friday, currency experts said.
Tumbling asset prices, however, did much less damage than in times past, they said.
The dollar was steadied for much of the session by expectations of an eventual Federal reserve credit tightening after the release of strong U.S. retail sales and producer price data.

"It feels to me that linkage is clearly broken. High U.S. interest rates are clearly benefitting the dollar more than sales of U.S.-dollar-denominated assets (are hurting it)," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.
A falling dollar/Swiss weighed on dollar/mark, they said.

But the U.S. unit gained slightly against the yen, though support was fragile as the Dow industrials tumbled 148.36 points and U.S. bonds slumped on speculation that the robust U.S. economy was leading to inflation.
The dollar closed at 1.7210/20 marks, down from 1.7244/49 marks at the open. Against the Japanese currency, the dollar finished at 126.12/22, up marginally from 126.08/18.

Anticipation of higher rates was fueled partly by surprisingly robust retail sales data. February sales were revised higher to show a 1.5 percent gain that was much stronger than the previously reported 0.8 percent rise and the tame 0.2 percent increase in March.
Core producer prices rose 0.4 percent in March, after falling in February, also bolstering speculation about higher rates. Headline wholesale prices fell 0.1 percent in March.

"You have to own dollars for the interest rate differential, the economy is steaming ahead at three-to-four percent and inflation looks like it is going to be problem in the future," said Russell LaScala head of spot foreign exchange trading at Citibank.
The Swiss franc rose, meanwhile, weighing heavily on the dollar and the mark, with dealers pointing to tighter conditions in Switzerland's money markets as the reason.
"It seems as if some of this is purchasing of Swiss francs against both dollars and deutschemarks, pulling the dollar down," said ABN-AMRO's Nelson.
Dollar/swiss fell to 1.4605/15 from 1.4695/05 at the open and mark/Swiss eased to about 0.8495 from 0.8524.

The dollar rose briefly versus the yen in Tokyo after Japanese cabinet member Kabun Muto said any "artificial" attempt to to check further yen weakness could fail in the current environment of continuing capital outflow from Japan.

But Friday's rally was cut short after Japan's Ministry of Finance distanced itself from Kabun's remarks. The Ministry said the official view remains that the yen's falls are overdone and the goverment remains concerned about it, repeating the warning they have issued all week.
The dollar ignored remarks by Richmond Fed president Alfred Broaddus that the strong dollar makes U.S. firms reluctant to raise prices. He also said the dollar could weaken as the year unfolds.
It also shook off remarks by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel that the three-percent government deficit to economic growth target for European monetary convergence meant 3.0 percent.
The dollar ended at Canadian $ 1.3977/82, compared to 1.3930/35 at the open, after rising to a two-year high at 1.3985 despite Bank of Canada intervention.
The pound rose to $1.6270/80 from $1.6240/50 and the Australian dollar fell to $0.7845/50 from $0.7877/82.
((-- Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
